theme: The holiday visit: you can just visit. Go home to be together, not to run a list of checks.

posts.text:
A lot of holiday advice is a list of things to check on your parents when you visit.

I'd skip the list. Go home, eat the meal, play the game, listen to the stories.

Your parents are adults with their own plans. A visit can just be a visit.
posts.alt: Provisional, three-panel strip. Dana at her desk on the phone: I'll be there Thursday. Anything you need? Walt at his workbench by his bicycle, phone to his ear: Bring your appetite. And your chess game. Then the two of them at a kitchen table over a chess set, smiling, a green kettle on the stove. Caption: A visit can just be a visit.

posts.title: Going home for the holidays: let the visit be a visit
posts.text:
Three easy ideas for a holiday visit with your parents.

1. Ask what they want to do while you are there.
2. Join in on what they already do.
3. Let them lead the talk.

For checking in, not checking up.
posts.alt: Provisional, vertical three-panel strip. Walt opens his front door to Dana: You made it. Want to see the bike? Caption: Ask what they want to do. At his workbench, Dana holds a wrench: Show me what you're fixing. Caption: Join in on what they already do. At a diner counter with coffee, Walt: So. Tell me about your work. Caption: Let them lead the talk.

posts.text: Going home for the holidays? You can just visit. Apply for the family beta at heykettle.com.

script.say: A lot of holiday advice says: when you visit your parents, make a list of things to check.
I don't think a visit should feel like an inspection. Your parents are adults with their own plans.
I built Kettle for my own parents. It notices their normal day happened, using the phone they already own, and sends a short note twice a day.

posts.text:
The calls before a holiday visit turn into plans. Flight times, who's picking you up, what to bring.

Those calls help. Once you're there, let the plans stop for a while. Ask what's new with them, and listen.
posts.alt: Provisional, three-panel strip. Dana walking with a suitcase, on the phone: I land at four. Who's picking me up? Walt at a diner counter with the paper, phone to his ear: Me. I'll be the one with the beard. Then Walt hugging Dana beside his car at the curb. Caption: After that, just time together.

posts.title: Leaving after a holiday visit: three easy habits
posts.text:
Three easy habits for the end of a visit with your parents.

1. Say when you'll call next.
2. Leave things the way they like them.
3. Send a note when you get home.

Small things that make the distance feel a little shorter.
posts.alt: Provisional, vertical three-panel strip. Dana leaving Walt's front door with a suitcase: I'll call Sunday, same as always. Caption: Say when you'll call next. In the kitchen, Walt: Leave the dishes. I have a system. Caption: Leave things the way they like them. Dana on a bus, typing on her phone: Home now. Thanks for the chess lesson. Caption: Send a note when you get home.

posts.title: The day after the visit.
posts.text: The day after a visit, the distance comes back. For checking in, not checking up.

script.say: The day after a holiday visit, you're back home, and your parents are far away again.
That's often when the low, background worry comes back.
I didn't want to watch my parents. I wanted to know their normal day happened. So I built Kettle: a short note, twice a day.

script.say: If a morning isn't as usual, it asks them first. Before anyone else hears a thing.
